awd_titl_txt: RAPID: Household Responses to the Los Angeles Wildfire Emergency
awd_abstract_narration:
The objective of this Grants for Rapid Response Research (RAPID) project is to collect ephemeral data to better understand the evacuation experience of households affected by fast-moving urban wildfires in Pacific Palisades and Altadena, California. The project examines how people evacuate (travel mode, time, routes), where they find immediate shelter, and the effect of the evacuation experience on evacuees and their future housing decisions. Cities continue to develop in wildland-adjacent areas, greatly increasing community exposure to wildfires. The findings from this study provide the data to improve how households, emergency responders, and management agencies prepare for and respond to this growing threat.  

The increase in urban wildfires highlights the need to better understand human behavioral responses to them, an area of research with significant gaps. This RAPID project focuses on wildfire evacuation and collects survey data from a heterogeneous set of households affected by the two recent urban wildfires in Pacific Palisades and Altadena, California. The data are collected using a random sample of households in the most affected neighborhoods and a convenience sample collected through non-profit and community partners. The survey instruments include questions on evacuation (mode, routes, and experience), the evacuation experience, and shelter or housing destinations and type. The survey data are paired with information on the built environment in the evacuated neighborhoods and the location and timing of official evacuation notices. The survey, combined with other supplementary data, provide the foundation for improved behavioral models and serve as the basis for strengthening evacuation procedures in urban wildfires and other disasters.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Household Responses to the Los Angeles Wildfire Emergency

Project Outcomes Report

We administered two surveys—a random sample survey and a convenience sample survey—to collect data on the evacuation experience of a heterogeneous set of households affected by the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires in Pacific Palisades and Altadena, California.  The surveys were available to complete in both English and Spanish.  The grant was for data collection, cleaning, and assembly only.  The survey instrument included questions on travel behavior, shelter, and the evacuation experience.  

For the random sample survey, the survey firm randomly selected individuals in the two most severely affected zip codes, one in each wildfire area.  For the convenience sample, we contacted numerous organizations working in each of the wildfire areas and solicited their help in surveying their members.  We collected 712 respondents for the random sample and 535 for the convenience sample, figures above the numbers we included in our proposal. Table 1 summarizes the data by wildfire area and sample type.

For each respondent, we added information on the built environment in the neighborhood from which the survey respondent evacuated. We added from the US Environmental Protection Agency’s Smart Location Database block-group level variables including car ownership, residential, population, and activities densities, road network and intersection densities, distance to transit and access to frequent transit service, accessibility by car and by transit, and walkability.

Drawing on data from CalFire DINS, we matched more than three quarters of the respondents to the extent of structural damage in their neighborhood.  The categories are the following:  destroyed (over 50% damaged), major (26-50%), minor (10-50%), affected (1-9%), and no damage. Finally, using data from Los Angeles County, we identified the highest level evacuation alert for the fire zone in which each respondent lives.  

We created codebooks for both of the datasets:  random sample and the convenience sample.  

With funds from other sources, we produced two initial policy briefs—one for each wildfire area—based on data collected from the random sample survey.  The briefs are entitled “Household Responses to the Los Angeles Wildfire Emergency” and can be found here:  https://www.lewis.ucla.edu/project/los-angeles-wildfire-response/.  Once again with funds from other sources, the investigators involved in the data collection effort are currently conducting additional analyses of the data.  

As we stated in our proposal, we will share the survey data in the NHERI Data Depot without locational information and other personally identifiable information (PII) one-year after the start of data collection (July 2026) and in tandem with the submission of our final report to the NSF on the data collection effort.
